sections.t: 01 Sea terms, parts of the boat, rigging and sails

cards.q: Bow, stern, port, starboard — what does each mean?
cards.a:
Bow = the front.
Stern = the back.
Port = the left side facing forward (red).
Starboard = the right side facing forward (green).

cards.q: Which parts of the boat should you be able to point at on day one?
cards.a:
Mast — the tall spar standing up out of the deck.
Boom — the horizontal spar along the bottom of the mainsail, swinging across the cockpit at about head height.
Mainsail — the sail behind the mast.
Headsail — the sail in front of it.
Keel — the heavy fin bolted on underneath, in the water.
Rudder — the blade at the back that steers her.
Tiller or wheel — what your hands are on to move the rudder.
Winch — the metal drum you take turns of rope round to pull something in.
Block — a pulley.

cards.q: Forward, aft, fore-and-aft, athwartships — what does each mean?
cards.a:
Forward (say 'for'ard') is towards the bow, aft is towards the stern.
Fore-and-aft means along her, bow to stern.
Athwartships means across her, side to side.
'Go forward' is an instruction to walk up the deck; 'the foredeck' is where you end up.

cards.q: Amidships
cards.a: The middle of the boat, both fore-and-aft and athwartships.

cards.q: Beam (two meanings)
cards.a:
1. The widest part of the hull, and so the boat's width.
2. A direction at right angles to the fore-and-aft line: 'abeam'.

cards.q: Ahead, astern, abeam, abaft, forward of the beam
cards.a: Ahead in front. Astern behind. Abeam at 90° to the fore-and-aft line. Forward of the beam anywhere in the 90° from ahead to abeam. Abaft the beam anywhere from abeam to astern.

cards.q: Foredeck, sidedeck, coachroof, cockpit, companionway — where is each?
cards.a:
Foredeck — the deck forward of the mast.
Sidedeck — the strip of deck down each side.
Coachroof — the raised cabin top in the middle you walk beside, not on.
Cockpit — the well you sit and steer in.
Companionway — the steps and hatch down into the cabin.

cards.q: Heads, galley, saloon, forepeak, berth — what is each?
cards.a:
Heads — the toilet.
Galley — the kitchen.
Saloon — the main cabin where everyone sits.
Forepeak — the cabin right forward in the bow.
Berth — a bunk, and also the space the boat is tied up in.

cards.q: Bilge, sole, bulkhead
cards.a:
Bilge — the lowest internal space where water collects.
Sole — the cabin or cockpit floor.
Bulkhead — a transverse structural partition.

cards.q: Pulpit, pushpit, stanchions, guardrails, jackstay
cards.a:
Pulpit — the rail at the bow.
Pushpit — the rail at the stern.
Stanchions — the posts supporting the guardrails along the deck.
A jackstay is a wire or webbing line running fore and aft that you clip a harness tether to.

cards.q: Draught
cards.a: The vertical distance from the waterline to the lowest point of the keel — the minimum depth of water the boat needs.

cards.q: Air draught
cards.a: The height from the waterline to the highest point of the boat, usually the masthead including the aerial. What matters for bridges and overhead cables.

cards.q: Freeboard
cards.a: The vertical distance from the waterline to the deck edge.

cards.q: Why does a yacht not tip over when she heels?
cards.a: The keel is a lead or iron weight bolted under the hull, and it is a large fraction of everything the boat weighs. She leans, and then she stops leaning. A gust presses her over and the keel stands her back up, so heeling is normal and is not the boat starting to go over.

cards.q: Heel versus list
cards.a: Heel is a temporary lean caused by wind or crew weight. List is a permanent lean caused by unbalanced weight or flooding.

cards.q: The three rotational motions of a boat at sea
cards.a:
Roll — side to side about the fore-and-aft axis.
Pitch — bow and stern rising and falling.
Yaw — swinging left and right of the heading.

cards.q: What is a seacock, and what are you expected to know about them?
cards.a:
The valve on a hole through the hull — the sink drain, the heads, the engine's water intake. Shutting one is what stops the boat filling if a hose or a fitting lets go, so on day one find the heads and sink ones and work out which way each of them closes.
In normal use you leave every seacock exactly as the skipper set it: some boats keep them shut and open them to use, others leave them open at sea.

cards.q: Name the three sides and three corners of a mainsail.
cards.a:
Sides: luff (leading edge), leech (trailing edge), foot (bottom).
Corners: head (top), tack (bottom forward), clew (bottom aft).

cards.q: Standing rigging versus running rigging
cards.a:
Standing rigging is fixed and holds the mast up: forestay,
backstay,
shrouds,
spreaders,
chainplates.

Running rigging moves and controls the sails: halyards,
sheets,
reefing lines,
kicker,
topping lift,
cunningham,
outhaul.

cards.q: Halyard versus sheet
cards.a: A halyard hoists a sail (pulls it up). A sheet trims a sail (pulls it in or lets it out).

cards.q: Topping lift
cards.a: A line from the masthead to the end of the boom that holds the boom up when the mainsail is lowered or reefed.

cards.q: Genoa versus jib
cards.a: Both are headsails. A jib's clew does not reach past the mast; a genoa overlaps the mast and is larger. A furling headsail can be partly rolled to reduce area.

cards.q: 'Ease the kicker' — what are you easing?
cards.a: The kicker, also called the boom vang: the strut or tackle from the bottom of the mast to the underside of the boom. It holds the boom down. Ease it and the boom is free to lift; take it up and the boom comes down again.

cards.q: Windward and leeward
cards.a: Windward is the side or direction the wind is coming from (also 'weather side'). Leeward ('loo-ard') is the side or direction the wind is going to — the sheltered side. On a sailing boat the leeward side is the boom's side.

cards.q: Lee shore — and why it matters
cards.a: A shore onto which the wind is blowing. It is dangerous: the wind and waves push you towards it, and it gives no shelter. A weather shore, with the wind blowing off it, is the sheltered one.

cards.q: The forecast says 'northerly'. Where is the wind coming from?
cards.a: From the north. A wind takes its name from where it comes from, so a northerly blows out of the north and pushes you south.

cards.q: What do 'on the wind' and 'off the wind' mean?
cards.a: On the wind is sailing as close to the wind as the boat will go: sheets hard in, well heeled, and usually the wettest and slowest-feeling point of sail. Off the wind is anything further round than that, with the sheets eased. 'Head up' or 'come up' takes you towards the wind, 'bear away' takes you off it.

cards.q: The word 'tack' means three different things. What are they?
cards.a:
1. The manoeuvre of turning the bow through the wind.
2. The bottom forward corner of a sail, the one shackled down at the front.
3. Which side the wind is coming over: on port tack the wind is on the port side and the boom is out to starboard, and the other way round on starboard tack.

cards.q: What is the difference between a tack and a gybe?
cards.a: Both swap the wind from one side of the boat to the other. In a tack the bow turns through the wind, the sails flap through the middle and cross quietly. In a gybe the stern turns through the wind and the boom swings the whole way across, fast and hard. That is why a gybe is announced, controlled and ducked, and a tack is only announced.

cards.q: What are the commands for tacking and gybing?
cards.a:
Tacking: 'Ready about?' — crew confirm — 'Lee-oh' as you put the helm down.
Gybing: 'Stand by to gybe' — check the mainsheet and kicker are in and the boom controlled — 'Gybe-oh'. In both cases the point is that everyone knows what is about to happen.

cards.q: What does 'underway' mean?
cards.a: Not tied up, not anchored, not aground. You can be underway and drifting about with the engine off and no sails up.

cards.q: What is a knot?
cards.a: One nautical mile per hour.

cards.q: How far is a nautical mile, and why is everything measured in knots?
cards.a: About 1.15 land miles, or a little under 2 km — it is the unit every distance at sea is given in. Speed through the water is knots and so is wind speed, so 'six knots' on the log (the boat's own speedometer) and 'twenty knots' in the forecast are the same unit. Six knots is about a gentle jog, and that is about what a cruising yacht does.

cards.q: On a sheet, what do 'ease', 'harden in' and 'trim' mean?
cards.a:
Ease — let rope out, slowly and still under your control.
Harden in, or 'sheet in' — pull rope in so the sail comes closer to the middle of the boat.
Trim — adjust it either way until the sail sets properly. 'Trim the genoa' is not an instruction to pull it in hard.

cards.q: How do you bend a mainsail on?
cards.a:
Bending on means attaching a sail to the spars. Shackle the tack down at the gooseneck, where the boom meets the mast,
feed the foot into the boom groove and pull the clew out to the outhaul,
feed the luff slides or bolt rope into the mast track from the head downwards,
shackle the halyard to the head and check it runs clear of the spreaders,
then put sail ties on until she is wanted.

cards.q: How do you rig a headsail correctly?
cards.a:
Hank on or feed the luff into the foil from the tack up,
shackle the tack,
attach the halyard to the head making sure it is not twisted round the forestay,
lead both sheets outside the shrouds through the fairleads to the winches,
and put stopper knots in the ends.

cards.q: Why is the boat turned head to wind to hoist the mainsail?
cards.a: So the sail flaps down the middle of the boat instead of filling. A sail with wind in it jams its slides against the mast track and no amount of winching will get it up. Head to wind the boom is also central and the mainsheet can be free. Expect a lot of flapping and noise while you hoist — that is what it is supposed to do.

cards.q: What is your part in hoisting the mainsail?
cards.a:
Take off every sail tie and count them, because one left on will tear the sail or stop the hoist dead,
check the halyard is not wrapped round anything,
ease the mainsheet and the kicker,
haul hand over hand while it goes up easily,
take the last of it on the winch,
then let the topping lift off once the sail is carrying the boom.

cards.q: How much halyard tension does the mainsail want?
cards.a: Enough that the creases running back from the luff just disappear, and no more. Hard vertical wrinkles up the luff mean you have over-tightened it; loose scallops between the slides mean it is slack. More wind wants it tighter. Set it, then ask the skipper to look.

cards.q: How do you unroll a furling headsail?
cards.a: Keep a turn of the furling line on the winch or a hand on it the whole way, so the sail comes out under control rather than unrolling in one bang. Someone pulls the leeward sheet while the furling line is fed off the drum against that resistance, which is what makes the line lie in neat turns for next time.

cards.q: How do you furl a headsail away?
cards.a: One person pulls the furling line while the other keeps a turn on the sheet and lets it go grudgingly, so the sail rolls up tight instead of flogging its way in. Never let the sheet run free. Finish with the furling line cleated hard and both sheet tails coiled, or the sail will unroll itself in the night.

cards.q: What does reefing do, and what will you feel before the skipper calls for one?
cards.a: Reefing makes the sail smaller so the boat stands up and steers instead of lying over. Before the call comes she will heel far more, bury the leeward rail, feel heavy and hard on the helm, and start banging into waves rather than driving through them. Say what you are feeling. Whether to reef is the skipper's call, but nobody else is sitting where you are.

cards.q: How do you put a reef in with slab reefing?
cards.a:
Head up or heave to,
take up on the topping lift,
ease the kicker and the mainsheet,
drop the halyard to the mark,
hook or pull down the luff cringle at the tack,
tension the halyard,
haul in the leech reefing line to the clew,
tension the foot,
ease the topping lift and re-set the kicker,
then bear away and trim.

cards.q: How do you shake out a reef?
cards.a:
In the reverse order:
take up the topping lift,
ease the halyard slightly and the reefing line,
free the luff cringle,
then hoist the halyard fully,
re-tension the outhaul and kicker,
ease the topping lift,
and trim. Make sure the reefing line runs free so it does not tear the sail.

cards.q: What is a preventer and when do you rig it?
cards.a: A line from the end of the boom led forward to a strong point on the foredeck to stop the boom crossing in an accidental gybe. Rig it whenever you are running or on a broad reach, especially at night or in a swell.

cards.q: How many turns go on a winch, and which way round?
cards.a: Three turns before any load comes on, and clockwise — every winch on the boat turns the same way and there is no left-handed one. Put the first turns on while the rope is slack. Extra turns go on as the load builds, which is normal and you will be asked to do it — but add them with the back of your hand to the drum and your fingers well clear of where the rope feeds on.

cards.q: What is tailing?
cards.a: Pulling in the rope that comes off the winch drum while somebody else winds the handle. Pull steadily and downwards, so the turns stay tight and stack down the drum. A loop standing proud of the others is a riding turn about to happen.

cards.q: What is a self-tailing winch, and when should you not use the self-tailer?
cards.a: The jaw on the top grips the rope so one person can wind and tail at once. Feed the rope up through the arm into the jaw after the turns are on. Take it out of the jaw before you ease anything under load — the jaw is designed not to let go, which is the opposite of what easing needs.

cards.q: Where do your hands go near a loaded winch?
cards.a: Flat on top of the turns, pressing down, and nowhere else. Never wrap a sheet round your hand and never put fingers where the rope feeds onto the drum. A genoa sheet in a gust does not stop for a finger. If a rope is running away from you, let it go and shout — do not grab at it.

cards.q: Riding turn
cards.a: A turn of rope trapped over itself on a winch drum so it will not release. Take the load off with a rolling hitch onto a spare line, then clear it.

cards.q: What causes a riding turn, and how do you keep from making one?
cards.a: Turns put on loosely, a rope led upwards into the drum instead of level or slightly below, or slack tailing that lets one loop climb over another. Keep the lead low, keep the tail pulled down and tight, start with three turns and add the fourth only once the load is already on.

cards.q: What do you do with the winch handle when you have finished with it?
cards.a: Take it out and put it back in its pocket, every single time. Left in the winch it gets kicked overboard or catches somebody's shin the moment the boat lurches.

cards.q: What is the difference between 'ease the sheet' and 'let it fly'?
cards.a:
Ease — let rope out slowly with the turns still on the winch and the load still yours.
Let it fly — take the turns off and let the sheet go completely, so the sail flaps and all the drive comes off at once. Letting fly is a stop button for a sail. Do it only when you are told, because the rope end whips and the sail flogs.

cards.q: What does 'sweat it up' mean?
cards.a: Getting the last of a halyard up with two people and no winch. One hauls the halyard sideways away from the mast and lets it back to the cleat, the other takes in the slack that appears each time it goes soft.

cards.q: How do you stow the mainsail once it is down?
cards.a: Take up the topping lift first so the boom cannot drop on anybody. Then flake the sail from side to side over the boom in folds, working outwards from the middle, pulling the leech and the foot straight as you go — a stuffed sail comes out full of creases next time. Finish with sail ties round boom and sail about every arm's length.

cards.q: Warp, spring, breast line
cards.a: Warps are mooring lines: bow line and stern line run forward and aft. Springs run at a shallow angle to stop fore-and-aft movement. Breast lines run at right angles to hold the boat in to the pontoon.

cards.q: Fenders, fairleads, cleats and bollards
cards.a: A fender cushions the hull. A fairlead guides a line and takes the chafe. A cleat or bollard is what you make the line fast to. Never lead a warp over a sharp edge.

cards.q: What does 'make fast', 'belay', 'surge' and 'snub' mean?
cards.a:
Make fast / belay — secure a line.
Surge — let a line slip in a controlled way round a winch or cleat.
Snub — check a running line sharply to take the load.

cards.q: What are the three parts of a rope you name when tying knots?
cards.a:
The standing part (the loaded main length),
the bight (a bend or loop in it),
and the working end (the end you tie with). The extreme end is the tail; strictly, the bitter end means the inboard end of the anchor cable, made fast at the bitts.

cards.q: Figure of eight — use
cards.a: A stopper knot in the end of a sheet or halyard so it cannot run out through a block or fairlead.

cards.q: Clove hitch — use and limitation
cards.a: Attaches a line to a rail, post or ring — the classic fender lanyard knot. It can slip or work loose under a varying or uneven load, so it is not for a load-bearing mooring line.

cards.q: Rolling hitch — use
cards.a: Grips along another rope or a spar. The standard fix for a riding turn on a winch or a jammed sheet: tie it to the loaded line and lead it to another winch to take the strain.

cards.q: Bowline — use
cards.a: Makes a fixed loop that will not slip and can be untied after loading. Used to attach a sheet to a clew, drop a loop over a post, or make a temporary loop anywhere.

cards.q: Round turn and two half hitches — use
cards.a: Secures a mooring line to a ring, post or bollard. The round turn takes the load, so it can be tied and untied while the line is under tension.

cards.q: Reef knot — correct use and the trap
cards.a: Joins the two ends of the same line of equal diameter — tying in a reef, a sail tie, a lashing. It is not a knot for joining two ropes under load: use a sheet bend or a double sheet bend.

cards.q: Sheet bend and double sheet bend
cards.a: Join two ropes together. Use the double sheet bend when the ropes differ in size or are slippery — the extra turn stops the thinner one pulling through.

cards.q: You are handed a warp and told to make it fast on a cleat. What is the sequence?
cards.a:
A full turn round the base of the cleat first, taken to the far horn rather than the near one so the rope cannot jam on itself. That turn holds the load while you do the rest.
Then figure-of-eight turns across the horns, diagonally over the middle — three or four of them in modern slippery line, not one.
Leave the tail lying fair and free, never buried under a coil, so the next person can let it go in the dark.

cards.q: Do you finish a cleat with a locking hitch?
cards.a: Ask, because practice genuinely differs and you will meet both. A locking hitch — the last turn twisted so it traps the tail — is normal on a mooring warp that is going to sit there for a week. It is wrong on anything you may have to release while it is loaded: a halyard, a sheet, or your line on a shared bollard that another crew may need to cast off. It is a deliberate jam, and a jam has to be picked out at the moment you least have time.

cards.q: How do you make a line fast to a bollard?
cards.a:
Single bollard, meaning one post: a bowline dropped over the top if the line can be tied before the load comes on, a round turn and two half hitches if it cannot.
Double bollard, two posts or one with a cross-bar: lead the line in a figure of eight round the two heads, crossing between them each time, and finish with a turn. The crossed turns hold each other down; turns dropped straight over one head lift off the moment the line goes slack.

cards.q: Somebody else's mooring line is already on the bollard. Where does yours go?
cards.a: Not on top of it. Pass the eye of your line up through theirs from underneath, then drop it over the post — this is dipping the eye. Both eyes sit on the bollard and either boat can lift its own off without disturbing the other. Drop yours straight on top and you have moored the boat that got there first to the quay until you come back.

cards.q: You are told to let a warp out under control while the boat moves. How?
cards.a: With turns on, letting the rope slip round them: a round turn on the cleat, or two or three round a winch drum. The friction holds the boat, not your arms. Lean back, feed it out, add a turn for more grip and take one off for less. To stop it, snub it — hold the tail hard in against the turns and let the rope pull up short. Keep your hands an arm's length back from the cleat or the drum, and never try to hold a loaded rope on grip alone.

cards.q: How do you throw a line to somebody ashore?
cards.a:
Make your own end fast on board first, or stand on it, or the whole rope goes in the water with the throw.
Coil it down loosely, then split the coil: about a third in the throwing hand, the rest in the other hand held open so it can run.
Shout, wait until they are looking, and throw the small coil over them or just past them rather than at them.
Never with a hand through the coil.
If you miss, pull it in and coil it again — a rope left floating goes under the boat and round the propeller. And if you can step ashore, step rather than jump.

cards.q: How do you spot a badly led rope before the load comes on?
cards.a: By looking along the whole run of the line while it is still slack, because afterwards you cannot fix it. A line that turns a corner on the way to its fairlead, chafes on a stanchion, or crosses another line under load is badly led. On a cleat, a turn taken to the near horn first, or a tail trapped under the loaded part, locks solid and will not come off when it is wanted. A rope that will not render when you ease it is telling you the same thing. Take the load off it and start again.

cards.q: Why do you never put a hand or a finger inside a loop of rope?
cards.a:
Because a bight closes, and it closes faster than you can pull out of it. A loop lying loose round your hand or your foot becomes a noose the instant the rope comes tight, and people lose fingers this way every season. So no hand through a coil you are carrying or throwing,
no rope wrapped round a hand or a wrist for a better grip,
no standing inside the bight of a warp that is running out,
and stand outside the angle of a line under strain, never in it.

cards.q: Chafe — why is it the thing that actually breaks mooring lines?
cards.a: A rope under load moving over any edge wears through from the outside, often overnight and unseen. Use fairleads, chafe sleeves or a length of hose, and inspect lines where they pass over the toe rail.

cards.q: You are given a length of split hose to put on a warp. Where does it go?
cards.a: On the rope, at the exact point that touches the fitting, taped there so it cannot slide off as the boat moves about all night. Padding the fairlead or the toe rail instead achieves nothing — it is the rope that is being sawn through, so it is the rope that gets the jacket.

cards.q: How do you coil rope so it runs cleanly?
cards.a: Laid (three-strand) rope is coiled clockwise with a slight twist in each turn. Braided rope prefers a figure-of-eight flake, which puts in no twist. A rope that has been coiled the wrong way will kink and jam in a block.

cards.q: The line is made fast. What happens to the rest of the rope?
cards.a: It gets made up. Coil the tail, reach through the coil and pull a bight of the loaded part through, twist it, and drop that loop over the cleat horn — the coil hangs off the loaded part, so it can be shaken free and let run without lifting it off first. Nothing is left in a heap on the sidedeck and nothing hangs over the side: a tail in the water finds a propeller, and it does not have to be yours. Ropes then live coiled, dry and out of the sun, and nobody stands on them.

cards.q: What is a slipped line, and why use one?
cards.a: A line taken round a cleat or ring ashore and back to the boat, so the crew can release it from on board without anyone going ashore. It is how you leave a berth or a buoy short-handed.

cards.q: How do you rig for a lock?
cards.a: Fenders both sides, long bow and stern lines ready to loop over the bollards or a ladder rung, and one crew on each. Keep the lines slipped from on board and tend them as the water level changes — never make fast solid in a rising or falling lock.

cards.q: What three things does a fire need?
cards.a: Fuel, air and heat — the fire triangle. Take away any one of them and the fire goes out. That is all any firefighting on a boat is doing: a fire blanket takes away the air, water takes away the heat, and shutting off the gas or the fuel line takes away the fuel.

cards.q: Where do fires actually start on a yacht?
cards.a:
The galley — a pan of fat, or a tea towel left over a lit ring.
The gas — a perished hose, or a ring turned on and not lit.
The engine bay — diesel or oil dripping onto a hot exhaust.
The electrics — chafed wiring behind a panel, a loose battery terminal, a charger left running.
Fuelling — petrol vapour off a spilt outboard can.

cards.q: Why does a gas leak on a boat end up in the bilge?
cards.a: Cooking gas is heavier than air. In a house it would drift up and out of a window; on a boat it runs downhill, through the cabin sole, into the bilge — the lowest and least ventilated space you have. It does not blow away. It sits there and waits for a spark.

cards.q: You smell gas below decks. What must you not touch?
cards.a: Anything electrical. Do not switch something on or off, do not start the engine, and do not run the bilge pump — every switch makes a small spark, and the bilge is exactly where the gas has gone. Turn the gas off at the bottle, open the hatches and washboards, get everyone on deck, tell the skipper.

cards.q: What is the routine every time you finish at the cooker?
cards.a: Turn the gas off at the bottle first and leave the burner alight until the flame dies on its own, then turn the ring off. That empties the hose, so a joint that weeps overnight has nothing left to leak. Turning the ring off first leaves the whole line sitting there charged.

cards.q: How do you fight a galley fat fire?
cards.a: Turn off the gas at the bottle or isolator, smother the pan with a fire blanket, and leave it covered to cool. Never use water on burning fat and never carry a burning pan through the boat.

cards.q: Why never throw water at an electrical fire?
cards.a: Water conducts, so you and the bucket become part of the circuit. Kill the power first — at the breaker if you know which one, at the battery isolator if you do not — and then use the dry powder extinguisher.

cards.q: What should you find on your boat before you sail, and where will it be?
cards.a:
The extinguishers, usually one at the companionway and one forward — sited so there is always one between you and a way out, never one you would have to reach across the fire to get.
The fire blanket, in the galley within arm's reach of the cooker but not hung directly over it.
Take each one off its bracket once in daylight, so your hands know how it comes off in the dark.

cards.q: The engine bay is alight. What is the one thing you must not do?
cards.a: Do not lift the engine box or the companionway steps. It is short of air in there; open it and you hand the fire a lungful, and it comes out at you. Stop the engine, shut off the fuel and the gas, leave the space shut, and shout for the skipper.

cards.q: What are the rules about smoking on board?
cards.a: On deck only, never below, and never near the gas locker or while a fuel filler cap is off. Sit on the leeward side so ash and sparks blow over the side rather than down the coachroof, and put the butt out in a tin — not over the side and not into a cockpit locker.

cards.q: You find a fire. What do you do, in order?
cards.a:
Shout — the word 'fire', loud enough for the whole boat, and say where it is.
Lifejackets on.
Everyone on deck, and upwind of the smoke.
Pass up the nearest extinguisher or the blanket.
Count heads.
Then do what the skipper tells you. Whether to fight it is the skipper's call, and smoke below decks will have you down long before the flames get to you.

cards.q: Lifejacket or buoyancy aid: what is the difference, and what rating do you want for cruising?
cards.a: A lifejacket — 100 N is the lowest lifejacket level, for sheltered water with prompt rescue at hand; 150 N for coastal and offshore use; 275 N for extreme conditions or heavy clothing — is designed to turn an unconscious wearer face-up and support them. A buoyancy aid is 50 N, inshore, and only helps a conscious person stay afloat: it will not turn an unconscious person face-up. Cruising calls for at least 150 N, with a crotch strap, light, whistle, spray hood and preferably an AIS beacon or PLB.

cards.q: Is there a law that says you must wear a lifejacket?
cards.a: On a private boat in the UK, generally no — what exists is guidance, not a statute. What actually binds you is the skipper's rule on that boat: the skipper says when lifejackets and harnesses go on, and aboard their boat that is not a suggestion. Some countries, and most charter companies, do make it a requirement, so ask before you sail.

cards.q: When should the crew wear lifejackets and harnesses?
cards.a:
Whenever the skipper says so — and as a minimum at night,
in poor visibility,
in rough weather,
when reefing or working on deck,
in a dinghy,
and for non-swimmers and children. Clip on before you leave the cockpit at night.

cards.q: Why does a lifejacket need a crotch strap?
cards.a: Because the inflated jacket floats and you do not. Without the strap it rides up while you slide down inside it, and you end up wearing it round your ears with your face in the water.

cards.q: What do you check on your own lifejacket before you sail?
cards.a:
The gas bottle screwed in hand tight, with no rust and no white powder on it.
The firing indicator showing green, not red.
The service date.
The crotch strap there, and both buckles working.
The whistle on its lanyard, and the light — press it.
No tears in the cover.
Anything wrong with any of it, say so while you are still alongside.

cards.q: Automatic or manual inflation — which have you got, and why does it matter?
cards.a: An automatic jacket fires by itself within seconds of hitting the water. A manual one fires only when you pull the toggle. Both have the toggle, and both have an oral tube so you can top it up by mouth. Find out which yours is and where its toggle sits before you leave the pontoon.

cards.q: Where may you clip a tether, and where must you never clip it?
cards.a:
Clip on inside the cockpit, before you go out on deck, and stay clipped: to a jackstay, or to a strong point put there for the purpose — a padeye in the cockpit, a U-bolt at the mast foot.
Never to a guardrail, a stanchion, a grab rail or a shroud. Guardrail wire and its fittings are made to stop you leaning off the boat, not to catch a falling adult, and under that load they let go.

cards.q: Why does a tether have two hooks?
cards.a: So that you are never unclipped while you are moving. Clip the free hook on ahead of you, then unclip the one behind — there is always one on. Where the two legs are different lengths, use the short one on the foredeck, short enough that you cannot get to the water.

cards.q: One hand for yourself, one hand for the ship — what does it mean?
cards.a: One hand is always holding the boat; the job gets the other one. If it needs both hands, sit down, wedge yourself in, or clip on first. What a lurch takes is your feet, not your grip.

cards.q: What should be on your hands and feet on deck?
cards.a:
Feet — deck shoes or boots with a soft non-marking sole and a real grip pattern. Never bare feet: a cleat or a genoa track breaks toes. Never smooth soles on a wet deck.
Hands — sailing gloves whenever you handle loaded rope. A sheet running out through a bare hand takes the skin off it, and then you let go of something you needed to hold.

cards.q: Why is staying warm and dry a safety matter rather than a comfort one?
cards.a: Because cold makes you clumsy, slow and stupid, and it does all three before you notice any of them. Most of the bad calls made on deck belong to someone who got wet three hours earlier. Layers and waterproofs go on before you need them — once you are wet you will not get warm again at sea — and wear a hat.

cards.q: Someone goes over the side. What do you shout?
cards.a: 'MAN OVERBOARD' — those words, at the top of your voice, and keep shouting until somebody answers you. Not their name, not 'help'. It is the one phrase everyone on board has been briefed to react to, and it says what has happened without anybody having to ask a question first.

cards.q: What is the pointer's job?
cards.a: One person points at the casualty with a straight arm and does nothing else at all — not a rope, not a switch, not fetching anything — until the casualty is back on board. A head in the water is the size of a football and shows for about a second at a time between waves. Glance away to be useful and you will not find it again.

cards.q: What goes over the side, and how soon?
cards.a: Everything that floats, at once: danbuoy, horseshoe lifebuoy, cockpit cushions, a fender. It gives the casualty something to hold and something to be seen by, and it marks roughly where they are. Throw it even if it lands nowhere near them — it drifts with the water they are in, while the boat is already somewhere else.

cards.q: What is a danbuoy for?
cards.a: It marks a man overboard with a visible flag on a weighted pole, often with a light, drogue and horseshoe lifebuoy. It gives the helm something to steer back to — a head in the water is almost invisible at any distance.

cards.q: What does the MOB button do, and who presses it?
cards.a: It drops a mark on the plotter at the position and time it was pressed, so there is a spot to steer back to when there is nothing left to see. Anyone presses it — whoever is nearest. Press it early, and press it again if you are not certain it took.

cards.q: Cold water shock — what does it do, and why does it kill before hypothermia does?
cards.a: The first minute is the one that kills. Cold water makes you gasp involuntarily and then breathe fast and hard, and you cannot stop either; if your head is under when you gasp, you inhale water. Remember 1-10-1: about one minute of gasping, then roughly ten minutes in which your hands and arms still work well enough to grab a line or a ladder — use them — and about an hour before hypothermia takes your consciousness. Being a strong swimmer barely helps.

cards.q: You are the one in the water. What do you do?
cards.a: Get your back to the waves, lean back, put your legs up in front of you, let the lifejacket hold your head clear, and float until the gasping stops — roughly a minute. Then knees up and arms crossed over your chest, the HELP position, which slows how fast you lose heat. Do not swim after the boat: she is faster than you, she is coming back anyway, and swimming spends the warmth and grip you are going to need.

cards.q: The boat is coming back. What is the crew doing?
cards.a:
Still pointing.
Boarding ladder down.
A line ready with a big bowline already tied in it.
Clipped on before anyone goes to the rail.
And nobody gets into the water. A rescuer in the water is a second casualty.

cards.q: Why should the engine be out of gear before anyone comes alongside the hull?
cards.a: Because the propeller will kill or maim someone in the water. Neutral, and preferably stopped, before the casualty is anywhere near the stern or the boarding ladder.

cards.q: Why lift a MOB casualty horizontally if you can?
cards.a: Because prolonged immersion causes the blood to pool in the legs. Lifting vertically can drop the blood pressure and cause post-immersion collapse and cardiac arrest. Keep them horizontal during and after recovery, and handle them gently.

cards.q: Red parachute rocket flare, red hand flare, orange smoke, white flare — what is each for?
cards.a:
Red parachute rocket — distress, to attract attention over the horizon at night, burns high for about 40 seconds.
Red hand flare — distress, to pinpoint your position for a rescuer who is already close.
Orange smoke — distress by day, best for aircraft and helicopters.
White flare — not a distress signal: it warns another vessel of your presence to avoid collision.

cards.q: Where are the flares kept, and could you tell them apart in the dark?
cards.a: Usually in a sealed watertight canister or a labelled locker by the companionway, where they can be grabbed on the way out. Find yours on day one and open it in daylight. A hand flare and an orange smoke are short and fat and are held; a parachute rocket is long and thin and is fired; the white collision flare is the odd one out by feel — a slim tube like the parachute rocket but half its length — and is the one you must never confuse with a red.

cards.q: You have been handed a flare and told to fire it. What do your hands do?
cards.a:
Read the case. The instructions are printed on every one of them and no two makes fire alike, so read them in daylight rather than at the moment.
Gloves on. Back to the wind, standing on the downwind, leeward side.
A hand flare or an orange smoke is held out at arm's length over the water, angled away from you, the boat and the rig, and left to burn.
Do not look at it, and never let anybody look into the end of a tube.
What comes off a burning flare is hot slag: molten residue that drips, and it goes through a deck, a sail bag, a dinghy, a liferaft and you. That is the reason for the glove and the arm over the side.

cards.q: Why is a red flare not a firework?
cards.a: Because a red flare says one thing — a life is in danger here — and anyone who sees one is obliged to act on it. One red seen from a beach launches a lifeboat, and can launch a helicopter. You fire one when the skipper says to, and for nothing else: not to celebrate, not to test, not to entertain.

cards.q: You need to signal distress and have nothing in your hands. What do you do?
cards.a: Stand where you can be seen and slowly raise and lower both outstretched arms at your sides, over and over. It is a recognised distress signal, it needs no equipment, and it works because nobody else waves like that. At night, flash a torch at whoever might be looking.

cards.q: There is a radio on board. What do you actually need to know about it?
cards.a:
It is a VHF set, and it is how the boat calls other boats, a marina, or the coastguard when help is wanted. Channel 16 is the distress and calling channel, and it is what the set is normally left listening to.
Sending a distress call is the skipper's job and needs a licence of its own. If you are ever told to make one, somebody will tell you exactly what to say — write it down and read it out.
Otherwise you do not touch the radio unless you are asked to.

cards.q: What is the distress beacon on board, and what is your part in it?
cards.a: A small transmitter: an EPIRB registered to the boat, or a PLB registered to a person and carried in a pocket or on a lifejacket. Switched on, it tells the rescue services who you are and where you are, anywhere in the world. Your part is knowing where it lives, and taking it with you if the boat is ever left.

cards.q: What goes in a grab bag?
cards.a:
Handheld VHF,
EPIRB or PLB,
handheld GNSS,
flares,
torch,
whistle,
water,
high-energy food,
first aid and seasickness tablets,
thermal protective aids,
sun protection,
a knife,
a hand bailer,
spare glasses and any essential medication,
plus passports and ship's papers if there is time.

cards.q: The order comes to abandon to the liferaft. What is your part in it?
cards.a:
You go when the skipper says to go, and not before: the yacht is a better liferaft than the liferaft is, for as long as she is floating.
Lifejacket on and done up.
The grab bag comes out with you.
Step up into the raft off the deck if you can and stay dry — a soaked person in a raft is cold within minutes.
Count heads out loud as people arrive.

cards.q: The liferaft's painter — what is it, and why does it go on first?
cards.a:
The painter is the long line out of the raft, and it does two jobs: it holds the raft to the yacht, and it is the lanyard you haul on to fire the gas bottle. So it is made fast to a strong point on the boat before the raft goes over the side, every time, and it is cut only once every single person is aboard.
The raft goes over the leeward side, where the hull gives it a lee and it lies alongside for you to step into. A raft is all windage and no draught and drifts downwind faster than the yacht does, so one launched to windward blows straight back onto her and ends up against the topsides or under the hull.

cards.q: How do you launch and board a liferaft?
cards.a:
Secure the painter to a strong point on the boat,
throw the raft over the leeward side,
pull the painter hard to fire the gas bottle,
board dry from the deck if you can,
get everyone in,
then stream the drogue,
close the canopy,
cut the painter and bail out. Take seasickness tablets early.

cards.q: What is the ensign, where is it worn, and when does it come down?
cards.a:
The flag that shows the boat's country of registry, and it takes the most senior position on board: as near the stern as you can get it, on a staff on the transom or clipped to the backstay when the staff is in the helmsman's way. A UK boat wears the Red Ensign; other ensigns need special permission, held through a particular club.
It is up in daylight, particularly near land or in sight of another vessel, and a UK boat must wear it entering or leaving a foreign port. At night it comes in and gets stowed, rather than being left wrapped round the staff to chafe and fade.
Note the verb: an ensign is worn. Every other flag on the boat is flown.

cards.q: What is a burgee, and where does it fly?
cards.a: A small triangular flag showing which club the owner or skipper belongs to. Traditionally at the masthead, but the masthead of a modern boat is full of instruments and a wind vane, so it usually flies from the starboard spreader instead — and it shifts to the port spreader when a courtesy flag needs the starboard one. Only one burgee flies at a time.

cards.q: Two flags fly from the starboard spreader. What are they, and who decides when?
cards.a:
The courtesy flag — the maritime flag of the country you are visiting, with nothing above it on that halyard. No law requires one; it is a courtesy, which is why a faded, frayed or comically small one reads as an insult. Coming the other way, a visitor to any part of the UK flies the Red Ensign, not the Union flag.
The plain yellow Q flag — hoisted arriving from abroad to say the boat is healthy and is asking for customs and health clearance, and left up until the skipper has finished reporting. Nobody goes ashore before that is done.
What each country wants differs and changes, so the skipper says which flag goes up and when. Your part is bending it on the halyard the right way up.

cards.q: It is 2300 in a full marina. What noise are you responsible for?
cards.a:
Halyard slap before anything else — a slack halyard tapping an alloy mast is a bell, and it keeps a whole pontoon awake. The fix is to pull the tail away from the mast and set it up hard, out to a shroud, the toerail, the pushpit or the boom end. Clipping it to the pulpit and leaving it loose achieves nothing.
After that:
charging on the engine or a generator early or late;
music in the cockpit, which every boat around you hears as well as you;
a wind generator left spinning;
hatches and washboards dropped rather than placed;
the chain run out over the roller at dawn;
a tender driven fast through a quiet anchorage;
and voices, which carry over water far further than anyone believes — in a raft at night you are talking directly into somebody's bunk. Most marinas publish quiet hours, commonly 2200 to 0800, and most put halyards in the berthing conditions.

cards.q: Another yacht asks to raft alongside you. What happens?
cards.a:
The answer is almost always yes — everyone needs a berth and refusing is poor form — but it is the skipper's call, not yours: the harbourmaster may cap the raft, often at three, and a yacht far heavier than you in a blow is a real reason to say no.
Fenders already out along your outside are the signal that you may come alongside.
Your part starts once she is coming: fenders down at her toerail height, and take her lines.
Then somebody settles the one thing that actually matters between the two boats: who is leaving, and at what time. An early start changes what everybody has to rig, and nobody wants to discover it at 0500.

cards.q: You are rafting onto another yacht. What goes on, and in what order?
cards.a:
Ask permission first, then:
fenders at toerail height, because you are fending off topsides and not a wall, made fast to the toerail rather than the guardwires, and bunched where the two hulls actually touch;
bow and stern lines onto her, and springs, so you cannot surge back and forth;
then your own bow and stern lines led past her to the pontoon, so that your weight is carried by the shore and not by her cleats, and say so once they are on;
shift fore or aft until the two masts are not level, because rigs at the same height will find each other in any chop;
and keep your rope tails on your own deck.

cards.q: You are on the outside of a raft. How do you get ashore?
cards.a:
Across each boat's foredeck, forward of the mast, one person at a time. Never through a cockpit. A cockpit is somebody's sitting room.
Go quietly, and more quietly after dark: no shortcut over the sprayhood, watch for open hatches, poles and low guardwires, and do not stop for a conversation hanging off a stranger's rigging.

cards.q: What must never go over the side?
cards.a:
Plastic, absolutely and everywhere: bags, film, packaging, rope ends, cable ties, a cigarette filter.
Oil, and anything with oil in it — a filter, an oily rag, the water under the engine.
Rubbish of any kind. Food scraps are the one exception, and only well offshore.
Chemical toilet contents, old antifouling, dead batteries and out-of-date flares all come ashore to somewhere that will take them.
Sewage from the heads is the one that is not a flat yes or no: it depends where in the world you are, so ask.

cards.q: Where may the heads be emptied?
cards.a:
It depends where you are, so ask — but the version that is never wrong is: not in a marina, a harbour or any enclosed water, and not on UK inland waterways, where it is prohibited by law.
Use the shore toilet where there is one, or the boat's holding tank and a marina pump-out.
At sea, well offshore, where it disperses. The Green Blue's advice is to get more than 3 miles out and to stay away from shellfish beds and anywhere with poor tidal flushing — that is best practice, not UK law.
Abroad it very often is law, the limits differ from country to country, and they have been tightening for years. Whoever is planning the trip checks the country you are going to.

cards.q: You are helping to refuel and there is diesel on the water. What must you not do?
cards.a:
Reach for the washing-up liquid. Detergent does not clean up a spill — it breaks it into droplets nobody can recover and pushes it down into the water, so the slick disappears and the damage does not. Use the absorbent pads in the spill kit.
Not making the spill is the real job: a big funnel or a collar round the nozzle to catch blow-back, and stop short of the brim, because fuel expands.
The same rule covers the boat's other poisons. Oily bilge water goes into a container, not over the side, and antifouling scrapings and wash-down are caught on a sheet ashore, because the coating is toxic on purpose.

cards.q: Why does it matter where the anchor goes down?
cards.a:
Because chain sweeps. Seagrass is nursery ground for fish and one of the fastest-disappearing habitats there is, and an anchor and its chain scour and break it up, then raise sediment that settles on whatever survived. A swinging mooring wears a bare circle in it over the years.
So sand or mud in preference to weed, and use the eco-moorings where somebody has gone to the trouble of laying them. Finding the seagrass is the skipper's job. Knowing why it is being avoided is yours.

cards.q: What is your responsibility about wash and speed?
cards.a:
Your wash is your responsibility. Slow down past moorings,
dredgers,
works,
small craft,
rowers,
swimmers and anyone working on a boat, and observe harbour speed limits — usually 6 knots or less, and often measured over the ground.

cards.q: How should you behave around marine wildlife?
cards.a:
Do not chase, encircle or separate animals;
keep a steady slow course and let them approach you;
avoid seal haul-outs and nesting seabird colonies, especially in the breeding season;
and give whales and dolphins a wide, predictable berth.

cards.q: What is a lookout for, and what do you keep it with?
cards.a:
Eyes and ears. Sight first, but hearing counts and is written into the rules for a reason — in fog or round a headland you often hear an engine, a bell or a fog signal before you see anything. Binoculars, radar and AIS come after that, not instead of it.
Every boat keeps one, all the time, not only when there is something about. And the job is not simply to look: it is to work out whether anything out there is getting closer, and to tell the skipper.

cards.q: How do you actually scan?
cards.a:
All the way round, over and over, and including astern — a yacht doing 5 knots is overtaken by nearly everything afloat, and by the time somebody thinks to look behind, an overtaking ship can already be close.
Stand up and move. Sitting in one corner of the cockpit you are watching one sector of the sea.
The blind spot on a yacht is the genoa. It hides a wide arc on the leeward bow, which is exactly where a converging ship sits, so duck down and look under the foot of the sail every few minutes.
And look close in as well as at the horizon: pot markers, kayaks, swimmers, a half-submerged log.

cards.q: How do you know you are on a collision course, with nothing in your hands?
cards.a:
Line the other vessel up against something fixed on your own boat — a shroud, a stanchion, the pushpit — and keep your head still. Wait a minute. Look again.
She has crept forward of the shroud: she will pass ahead of you.
She has slid aft of it: she will pass astern.
She is in exactly the same place and getting bigger: you are on a collision course. Tell the skipper now.
You do not have to be certain. If you cannot satisfy yourself that there is no risk, treat it as though there is one and report it.

cards.q: You have seen something. How do you tell the skipper?
cards.a:
Straight away, in a handful of words, and without deciding anything.
What it is, where it is, roughly how far — 'ship, two o'clock, about a mile'.
The clock runs round the boat, not the compass: twelve is dead ahead, three is out to starboard, six is astern, nine is out to port. 'Fishing boat on the port quarter' does the same job if that comes more naturally.
Report what you can see, not what you think it is going to do. Report it again if anything changes — and especially report that it has not changed. And report things you assume the skipper has already seen: saying it twice costs nothing.

cards.q: A big ship is coming up the channel. Why does that matter to you on the foredeck?
cards.a:
Because she can do almost nothing about you. A large ship takes over a mile and several minutes to stop, and much the same to turn, so by the time anyone aboard could see a problem it is too late to fix it. In a dredged channel she has no room to go anywhere anyway — you are the one with options.
And she may genuinely not be able to see you: the rules allow a blind sector ahead of her bow of up to 500 metres — a quarter of a mile of sea in which a small yacht is simply not visible from the bridge — and a small fibreglass yacht is a poor radar target as well.
So assume you have not been seen, and tell the skipper the moment you spot her, not when she is close.

cards.q: What does the tender's plate tell you, and how do you use it?
cards.a:
Most tenders carry a builder's plate, and the two numbers that matter are the maximum number of persons and the maximum load in kilograms — people, fuel, water, shopping and kit bags.
Small tenders under 2.5 m are outside the regulations and often have no plate at all. If there is none, ask the skipper what she is rated for and use freeboard as the test: if the side is close to the water, take somebody or something out.
Either way the plate figure is a maximum in calm water on a good day, not a target — if it is choppy, cold, dark, or any distance, take less and make two trips.

cards.q: Why is an overloaded tender the classic way people drown within sight of the marina?
cards.a: Because the freeboard goes. Freeboard is the height of the side above the water, and it is the entire margin against a wave or a passing boat's wash. Load the dinghy down and one wake comes over the side; it fills, and it loses stability and buoyancy at the same moment. A hard dinghy is worse than an inflatable, whose tubes still float when it is full of water. So keep the weight low and central, nobody perched on the tube or the gunwale, and put bags on the floor rather than on your back — a rucksack floats for a minute, then floods and holds you under.

cards.q: How do you get into a tender?
cards.a: One person at a time, and nobody moves until the one before is sitting down. The tender is held, or made fast bow and stern, before anyone steps. Step down into the middle of it, onto the floor or a seat, never onto the tube or the gunwale — it rolls away under your foot and puts you between two hulls. Keep low, and hold something above your waist: the shrouds, not a stanchion, because a low handhold levers you outboard instead of steadying you. Go down with empty hands and have the bags passed after. Look for wash coming before you start, and if it is marginal, do not do it at all.

cards.q: Who gets into the tender first, and who last?
cards.a: Somebody steady goes in first and stays sitting down to hold the dinghy against the boat, take the bags and steady each person as they arrive; the last one aboard is the one holding on until everybody else is settled. Boats and schools order it differently beyond that, so do what your skipper says — what never changes is that the tender is held the whole time and only one person is moving at once. If you are helping somebody in, offer a shoulder to lean on rather than a hand: a hand pulls you both over.

cards.q: Do you really wear a lifejacket for a two-minute row ashore?
cards.a: Yes, and that short familiar trip is the one people die on — at night, coming back, often after a drink, with nobody watching. Everyone in the tender wears one, every time, with the whistle and light on it. Do not take it off just because you are going ashore and would rather not carry it. Do not go alone if you can avoid it, and nobody drives a tender who has been drinking. One nuance for a small boat: a manually inflated jacket can be the better choice in a wet dinghy, because an automatic can fire on spray and leave you inflated in a boat you can no longer move about in.

cards.q: What are the rules about the painter?
cards.a: Painter is the general word for a small boat's bow line — the tender has one and so does the liferaft. The tender's is made fast before anybody gets in, and while you are alongside it is best held in somebody's hand, because a person soaks up the snatch that a hard-made line jerks against. Keep it short and inboard. Never let a bight of it trail in the water: a trailing painter is the thing that goes round a propeller. If the tender is on a tow astern, shorten it in before any close manoeuvring and always before the engine goes astern.

cards.q: How do you row a tender?
cards.a: Sitting on the thwart facing aft, so the dinghy goes the way your back is pointing. Both oars in the rowlocks, and the rowlocks tied on, before you push off — one dropped over the side ends the trip. Sit central with your feet braced and pull short even strokes; a short tender does not reward a long heave, it just slews. Look over your shoulder every few strokes, because you are facing away from everything you are about to hit. To turn on the spot, pull on one oar and push on the other.

cards.q: You are rowing to a landing with a tide running across you. Where do you aim?
cards.a: Up-tide of it, and further up than feels right, because you go where the tide takes you while you row and a tender does walking pace at best. Judge it against something ashore — line the landing up with something behind it and watch whether it stays in line — because the water gives you nothing to measure against. Same rule for wind: row out against it while you are fresh, so the tired leg home is the one being helped. If you are losing ground, get hold of something moored before you are set away, rather than rowing harder.

cards.q: What is a kill cord, and what does it prevent?
cards.a: A red coiled lanyard between the outboard's cut-out switch and the driver. If the driver is thrown away from the helm the cord pulls out and the engine stops. Without it, an outboard left running with nobody steering does not simply drive away — it turns and circles back through the people it has just thrown into the water. That is exactly what happened in the Camel Estuary in 2013, when six of one family went over the side and the boat circled back into them, killing two.

cards.q: Where does the kill cord clip, and where must it never clip?
cards.a:
Round your knee or thigh, clipped back onto itself, where it cannot foul the wheel or the throttle; on a jet ski, to the webbing of the buoyancy aid. Never to the console or a grab rail, which is the same as not having one.
Never round a wrist — it tangles in the wheel and slips off.
Never to clothing or a jacket you could come out of, because then the cord stays with the garment and the engine keeps running.

cards.q: What is the drill with the kill cord?
cards.a:
Test it at the start of each day: start the engine and pull the cord — the engine must stop. Look the lanyard over for wear, rust and stiffness while you have it in your hand.
Attach it to the driver before you start, and certainly before the boat goes into gear.
Changing driver: stop the engine. It is restarted only once the cord is secured to the new driver, never handed across while it is running.
A spare kill cord stays on board in a place the crew know about — if the driver goes over the side wearing theirs, the spare is the only way anybody restarts the engine to go and get them.

cards.q: What goes in the tender before you leave the yacht?
cards.a:
A lifejacket each, worn.
Oars and rowlocks even with an outboard, because the outboard is the thing that fails.
A bailer on a lanyard, and the pump if she is an inflatable.
The spare kill cord.
A waterproof torch.
A way of calling for help — a handheld radio, or a phone in a waterproof case.
Fuel actually checked rather than assumed.
A small anchor and line if you are going any distance.

cards.q: What is different about the tender at night?
cards.a: The torch stops being optional and it is the thing everyone forgets. It does three jobs: you can see what you are doing, you can pick your own yacht out of a mooring field of identical white boats, and you can shine it at anything coming towards you — a dinghy at night is invisible until you make it otherwise. Tell somebody on board where you are going and when you will be back, so that if you do not come back it is noticed while it still matters.

cards.q: What are Beaufort forces 0 to 3?
cards.a:
Force 0 calm, under 1 kn;
force 1 light air, 1-3 kn;
force 2 light breeze, 4-6 kn;
force 3 gentle breeze, 7-10 kn.

cards.q: What is the Beaufort scale, and what are forces 4, 6 and 8 called?
cards.a:
A scale of wind force from 0 to 12 based on observed sea state. Force 4 is a moderate breeze, 11-16 knots;
force 6 a strong breeze, 22-27 knots;
force 8 a gale, 34-40 knots.

cards.q: What are the wind speeds for Beaufort forces 5, 7 and 9?
cards.a:
Force 5 fresh breeze 17-21 kn;
force 7 near gale 28-33 kn;
force 9 strong gale 41-47 kn — which is the name on the Beaufort scale, though gale warnings and the shipping forecast call it severe gale 9.

cards.q: What are Beaufort forces 10, 11 and 12?
cards.a:
Force 10 storm, 48-55 kn;
force 11 violent storm, 56-63 kn;
force 12 hurricane force, 64 kn or more.

cards.q: Where can you get a marine forecast at sea?
cards.a:
Met Office shipping and inshore waters forecasts on BBC Radio 4 FM, DAB and BBC Sounds — the 198 kHz long wave transmission closed on 27 June 2026;
Maritime Safety Information broadcasts by HM Coastguard on VHF (announced on Ch 16, given on a working channel);
NAVTEX on 518 kHz;
the Met Office and other websites and apps by mobile data;
harbour offices and marina noticeboards;
and barometer plus your own eyes.

cards.q: When is the forecast looked at?
cards.a: Before you leave, so the skipper can decide whether to go at all, and again while you are out — a forecast is hours old by the time you are using it and the next one may not say the same thing. Getting it is often a crew job: write it down word for word as it is read out, do not summarise it, and hand it to the skipper.

cards.q: A gale warning is broadcast for the sea area you are in. What does that mean to you?
cards.a: A mean wind of force 8 or more, or gusts of 43 knots or more, is expected in that sea area within the forecast period. Whether the boat sails is the skipper's call and not yours; your part is to pass the warning on the moment you hear it, and then to expect a reef, lifejackets on and clipped on, hatches and washboards shut, everything below stowed properly, and hot food made early rather than later.

cards.q: The skipper asks what the wind is doing. How do you read it off the sea?
cards.a:
By what the water is doing, not by how cold you feel:
a few white horses breaking here and there — about force 3;
white horses everywhere and some spray coming off them — force 5 to 6;
foam blowing in streaks down the wind and spray stinging your face — force 7 and up;
the tops of the waves blown off into spindrift — force 8 and more. Report what you can see and let the skipper put a number on it.

cards.q: What brings seasickness on, and what makes it worse?
cards.a:
A disagreement inside your own head. Your inner ear feels the boat moving; your eyes, fixed on a cabin that is moving with you, report that nothing is happening. The brain cannot reconcile the two and makes you sick.
Everything that widens the gap makes it worse:
being below decks, where there is no horizon and the motion is greater the further you are from the middle of the boat;
reading, or a phone screen;
diesel, cooking and bilge smells;
cold and wet;
tired, hungry, hungover, or nothing eaten since breakfast.
It is not weakness and it happens to people who have sailed for thirty years.

cards.q: What actually helps?
cards.a:
Getting out into the air and putting your eyes on the horizon, which is the one thing in sight that is holding still.
Ask for the helm. Having a job to concentrate on plus something distant to look at is the best cure there is, and it works on people who are already green.
Small amounts of plain food, often, and water in sips — an empty stomach is worse than a full one, and dry biscuits exist for a reason.
Warm and dry clothing on before you need it.
Tablets work taken before you sail, at the interval on the packet. Once you are being sick nothing swallowed stays down long enough to help. Try any remedy ashore first: several of them make you drowsy, and a drowsy lookout is a different problem.
And say something early, while somebody can still do something about it.

cards.q: How do you deal with a crew member who is seriously seasick?
cards.a:
Take it seriously: it causes dehydration, poor judgement and accidents. Get them on deck in the fresh air,
low down and warm,
looking at the horizon,
with something in their stomach and a job to do such as steering. Clip them on,
keep fluids going,
and treat them as a casualty, not a nuisance. Tablets work best taken well before you sail.

cards.q: Name the points of sail, from head to wind round to dead downwind.
cards.a:
Head to wind — pointing straight at it, sails flapping, no drive.
Close hauled — as near the wind as she will sail.
Close reach — a little further off.
Beam reach — wind on the side.
Broad reach — wind over the back corner.
Run — wind from behind. Each of them exists on both tacks, so the same angle has a port and a starboard version.

cards.q: How close to the wind will a cruising yacht sail?
cards.a: About 45°, which leaves a wedge of roughly 90° centred on the wind that she cannot sail in at all — the no-go zone. Steer into it and the sails just flap. To get somewhere upwind you zig-zag across the wedge on one tack and then the other.

cards.q: Why does a sail pull the boat along, even going upwind?
cards.a: A sail is a wing lying on its side. Wind bending round the curve of it sucks the sail forwards and sideways at the same time. The keel is a big flat blade in the water that will not go sideways, so the sideways part is cancelled and what is left drives the boat forward. Downwind there is nothing clever about it — the wind is simply pushing.

cards.q: What is sail trim on the different points of sailing?
cards.a: Close hauled — sails hard in. Close reach — eased slightly. Beam reach — about half out. Broad reach — well out. Run — right out, boom well off and the headsail goosewinged or poled out. The rule is to ease until the luff just lifts, then pull in until it stops.

cards.q: What are telltales, and how do you steer to them?
cards.a: Short ribbons stitched near the front edge of the headsail, one each side. Both streaming straight aft means you are on course and the sail is working. The windward one lifting or dancing means you are too close to the wind: bear away a touch. The leeward one dancing means you are too far off: come up. Steer to the windward one and follow it with small movements.

cards.q: The front edge of the sail is fluttering. What is happening?
cards.a: The sail is luffing — wind is getting round the wrong side of its leading edge, either because you are steering too close to the wind or because the sheet is too far out. Bear away, or pull the sheet in. A sail left slatting hard is flogging, and flogging wrecks the stitching and shakes the whole rig, so it never gets left.

cards.q: The tiller is pulling hard against your hand. What is the boat telling you?
cards.a: That she is trying to turn up into the wind and you are holding her off it. That pull is called weather helm. Holding it means the rudder is sitting at an angle and dragging like a brake, so you are steering hard and going slower for it. Let some mainsheet out and see whether the tiller goes light. If it does not, say so, because from the helm you feel it before anybody else sees it.

cards.q: Which way do you push a tiller to turn the boat to starboard?
cards.a: To port. A tiller always goes the opposite way to where you want the bow to go; a wheel goes the same way, like a car. The way to hold it in your head is that the stern goes where you push and the bow does the opposite.

cards.q: How much should you move the helm?
cards.a: Hardly at all. A yacht answers slowly, so a beginner pushes, sees nothing happen, pushes further, and then has to haul it all back the other way — and the boat snakes down the sea for the rest of the watch. Move a little, wait for her to come round, then move again.

cards.q: What does your wake tell you about your steering?
cards.a: Look over the stern. A straight wake means you are holding a course; a snake means you are chasing it and over-correcting.

cards.q: The skipper says 'steer one-eight-zero'. What do you do, and what do you say?
cards.a: Say the number back — 'one-eight-zero' — so they know it was heard right. Bring her round until that figure sits under the mark on the compass and hold it. Then report honestly what you are actually managing: 'making about one-seven-five' is useful information.

cards.q: How do you hold a compass course without staring at the compass?
cards.a: Get her settled on the number, then pick something ahead that lines up with the bow — a headland, a chimney, the corner of a cloud — and steer at that instead. Glance down every few seconds to check the number has not crept. Clouds move and headlands come abeam, so choose a new mark when the old one stops working. Watching the compass alone means chasing the swinging card, and the boat wanders wider than if you looked up.

cards.q: Why is nothing metal put down near the steering compass?
cards.a: A phone, a torch, a tin, a winch handle or a toolbag left beside the compass makes it read wrong, and a wrong compass is worse than no compass because you go on steering the error perfectly. The shelf and the top of the binnacle — the compass housing — stay clear.

cards.q: What is different about steering under engine?
cards.a: There is no sail balancing her, so she wanders more and you correct more often. She only steers while water is moving past the rudder: in neutral, or barely moving, the helm does nothing at all and the wind blows the bow off where it likes. Going astern she steers badly and late, so make every turn earlier and bigger than feels necessary.

cards.q: How do you steer in a lumpy sea?
cards.a: Look at the water ahead rather than the instruments. Take the big ones slightly off the bow so she rides over instead of slamming, and come back to your course afterwards. Running downwind, keep the stern square to the wave behind so she does not slew sideways. A few degrees off course to miss a bad one is fine and nobody will mind.

cards.q: Why do you keep your head down when the boat is running?
cards.a: Because the boom is right out over the side, and one careless steer or one wave under the stern can bring it across the cockpit at head height. That is a gybe, and it arrives fast enough to put somebody over the side. Never sit under the mainsheet when running, and look at the boom before you stand up.

cards.q: Somebody is working on the foredeck. What does that mean for you on the helm?
cards.a: Hold her as steady and as level as you can, and warn them before anything changes: 'tacking in ten', 'big one coming'. No sharp turns, no gybe, no bearing away without telling them first and giving them time to get a hand on something. A movement that is nothing in the cockpit throws a person off their feet up there.

cards.q: What is a watch system, and what does a day on board look like?
cards.a:
The boat does not stop at night, so the crew is split into watches — groups who take the deck in turn while the others sleep. A watch is a shift: commonly two, three or four hours, often shorter through the night so that nobody gets all the cold ones. 'Your two hours' means your turn on deck.
So expect to be woken in the dark, to get dressed in a moving cabin, and to be on deck within a few minutes of somebody shaking your shoulder. Sleep when you are off watch even if it is the middle of the afternoon.
On a five-day course in daylight there may be no night sailing at all and the day is simply long. Ask on day one what the pattern is, when you eat, and where your bunk is.

cards.q: Somebody gives you an order and you do not understand it. What do you say?
cards.a:
'Say again.' Or 'I don't understand' or 'which rope?' — any of them, straight away and out loud. Asking is the correct thing to do and guessing is not: a wrong rope pulled hard costs a sail, and the person who asked has never yet been the problem.
Say what you cannot do, at the time: 'I can't reach it' now is worth far more than a failure in thirty seconds.
And people shout on boats. It is distance, wind and a flapping sail, not anger, and it stops the moment the noise does. Do not read a raised voice as a telling off.

cards.q: What may go down the heads?
cards.a: What you have eaten and drunk, and a little of the boat's own paper. Nothing else — no wipes, no sanitary products, no cotton buds, no kitchen roll, no food, no tea leaves. A yacht's heads is a small hand pump on a narrow pipe, not a house drain, and anything else stops it.

cards.q: You have used the heads at sea. What is the drill?
cards.a:
Pump it right through — a good many more strokes than you think, until the bowl and the whole pipe run clear;
put the lever or valve back the way you found it;
and leave the seacocks the way you found them too. If it blocks, say so straight away. Nobody comes out to a blocked heads — somebody on board takes the pump apart, in a seaway, and it gets worse the longer it is left.

cards.q: You are asked to make hot drinks under way. How do you do it safely?
cards.a:
One hand for yourself and one for the kettle, always.
Half fill it, so it cannot slop.
Let the cooker swing on its gimbals, the pivoting mount that keeps it level, and never grab it to steady yourself.
Brace against the cooker strap or a bulkhead, not against the pan.
Boots and sleeves on — a scald is the commonest injury below decks.
In a rough sea nobody goes below without a reason, and hot drinks may simply have to wait.

cards.q: You are told to 'stow everything' before leaving. What does that actually mean below decks?
cards.a: Everything has a place and goes in it: lockers latched, floorboards down, drawers shut, nothing standing on the chart table, no mugs, phones or books left on a shelf or a bunk. Heavy gear low down and near the middle of the boat. A winch handle left in a winch or a tin left on the galley top is a missile the first time she rolls, and she will roll further than you expect.

cards.q: When is a deck job actually finished?
cards.a: When the deck is clear. Every rope coiled and hung on its cleat or winch, every tail off the sidedeck, sail ties, boat hook and winch handles back where they live, and nothing left where a foot can catch it. A line in a heap goes over the side and round the propeller. A bight lying across the deck trips you at the exact moment the boat rolls.

cards.q: You are asked to check the bilge. What are you looking for, and what do you do?
cards.a: How much water is in it, and whether that is more than there was yesterday. A little is normal on most boats. A bilge that was dry this morning and is wet now gets reported to the skipper straight away — before you pump anything out. Smell it if you can — never taste it, because bilges collect diesel and engine oil: salt means it is coming in from outside, fresh means a tank or a hose.

cards.q: Why are the washboards in and the hatches shut at sea?
cards.a: Because a wave that breaks over the deck goes wherever it finds a hole, and the one hole that matters is the companionway. A boat knocked flat with the deck sealed comes back up; a boat knocked flat with the cabin open fills. Shut them behind you, and put the board back even when you are only nipping below for a minute.

cards.q: You are on watch at night while the skipper sleeps. What are you actually doing?
cards.a:
Steering the course you were given and holding it;
looking all round, including astern and to leeward behind the headsail, and at any light you were told to watch;
glancing over the instruments and the sails;
and staying awake — stand up, move about, and never keep the watch sitting below out of the wind. Nothing out there is yours to solve. Call the skipper for a ship that is not going away,
a change in the wind,
a new noise,
a light you cannot name,
or feeling ill or cold. Wake them early rather than once you are sure.

cards.q: Your watch is over. What do you hand over?
cards.a:
Where the boat is and where she is going, the course you have been steering, and anything the skipper told you to watch for;
what shipping is about and which lights you have been keeping an eye on;
what the wind and the weather have done in your two hours;
anything you changed, and anything odd you noticed;
and how far the log is filled in. Stay on deck until the person taking over is awake, dressed, clipped on and has their eyes in — not until they say they are coming.

cards.q: The skipper reads out the hourly log entry. What is your job?
cards.a: Write down exactly what you are given — the time, the position off the instruments, the course, the speed, the wind — in the boxes, in ink, at the time. Do not round the numbers, do not tidy them up, do not decide a line is not worth filling in because nothing happened. If the instruments fail, that column of numbers is the only record of where the boat has been.

cards.q: When do you get the fenders and warps ready for an arrival?
cards.a:
Before you get there, while there is still sea room and nobody is shouting. Fenders hung at the height of the pontoon, both sides if you have not been told which side you are going in;
bow line, stern line and springs led out through the fairleads, outside the guardrails, ends coiled and to hand;
boat hook out of its clips.

cards.q: Why should you check for lines in the water before starting the engine?
cards.a: Because a mooring line, sheet or MOB retrieval line round the propeller stops the engine, may damage the shaft and gland, and leaves you without power at the worst moment. It is the standard mistake in a man-overboard drill.

cards.q: What is the crew's part of the daily engine and battery check?
cards.a:
Before it is started: the raw-water seacock open, and a look in the bilge under the engine for oil or water that was not there yesterday.
Once it is running: go and look over the stern — cooling water should be coming out with the exhaust. If it is not, tell the skipper at once.
Batteries: switch off the lights, instruments and fridge nobody is using, and read out the voltage when you are asked for it. You look and you report. Nobody expects you to fix anything.

cards.q: Why should you never use your hands or feet to fend off?
cards.a: Because a few tonnes of boat crushes fingers and legs. Use a fender or a boat hook, and if the boat is going to hit, let it hit — the gel coat is cheaper than a hand.

cards.q: What is the discipline about fresh water and rubbish on board?
cards.a:
Water — the tank is all there is until you are next alongside. Pump rather than run the tap, wash up in a bowl, use sea water for the first wash and for the deck, and tell the skipper when a tank runs dry rather than quietly switching to the last one.
Rubbish — bag it and stow it below or lash it down, because a bag left in the cockpit goes over the side in the first gust, and all of it comes ashore to the marina bins.

cards.q: What do you pack for a week aboard, and what do you wear on deck?
cards.a:
Everything in a soft bag. There is nowhere on a yacht to put a suitcase, and a rigid one will be left on the pontoon.
Wear layers: a thin base layer, a fleece or two, then waterproof trousers and jacket over the top. No jeans and no cotton next to the skin — both hold water and take a day to dry.
Deck shoes or boots, and thick socks — wet feet are the first part of you to get cold.
A warm hat, and gloves, including a spare pair of both, because the first pair goes over the side.
Sun does more damage over water than on land: high-factor cream, a peaked hat, and sunglasses on a cord.
A complete second dry set of everything, in a drybag inside the soft bag.
Seasickness tablets bought before you travel, and a torch.
